question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A weather service that announces "rain tomorrow" and one that announces "a seventy per cent chance of rain tomorrow" may be relying on the same model, yet they are offering different things. The first has made a decision on the listener's behalf; the second has handed the decision back. For a long time public agencies preferred the first form, reasoning that ordinary users find probabilities confusing and want to be told what will happen. The preference is understandable, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what a forecast is for. A forecast has no value in itself; its value lies entirely in the decisions it improves. And the same probability should lead different users to different decisions. A farmer deciding whether to spray a pesticide that washes off in rain should hold back at a probability that a construction contractor, for whom an idle day is costly, would happily ignore. Each user has a threshold, set by the ratio of what it costs to protect against the event to what is lost if the event occurs unprotected, and a forecast is useful only if it can be compared against that threshold. A categorical forecast silently imposes a single threshold — the forecaster's — on everyone.

There is a second cost. A forecaster who must say yes or no will be judged by how often the yes comes true, and will learn to lean in whichever direction is less embarrassing. Warnings of cyclones and floods drift towards over-caution, until users learn to discount them. A probabilistic forecast can instead be checked for calibration: of all the days on which rain was given a seventy per cent chance, did it rain on about seventy per cent of them? A service that is well calibrated deserves trust even when it is wrong on a particular day, and its users can learn how far to rely on it.

None of this means that probabilities explain themselves. They must be accompanied by guidance on what they imply for common decisions. But the remedy for the public's unfamiliarity with uncertainty is to help people reason about it, not to conceal it.

Q. Which one of the following best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: (a) Weather agencies have deliberately misled the public by hiding the uncertainty in their models.

(b) Forecasts should state probabilities rather than verdicts, because a forecast's value lies in the decisions it informs, which depend on each user's own costs, and because probabilities can be honestly evaluated.
(c) Since ordinary users cannot understand probabilities, forecasts must always be simplified and accompanied by explanations.
(d) Probabilistic forecasts are more accurate than categorical forecasts because they are produced by better models.
explanation: The passage argues (i) the same probability should lead different users to different actions, so a yes/no verdict imposes the forecaster's threshold on all, and (ii) probabilities can be checked for calibration. (b) combines both strands. (a) imputes deliberate deception; (c) reverses the author's view (he rejects concealment); (d) contradicts the opening line — both may use the same model.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Main idea - forecasting as decision support (probabilistic vs categorical forecasts)

Q. The forecast for tomorrow gives a 30 per cent chance of rain. On the reasoning of the passage, for which one of the following users is taking protective action most clearly justified?
options: (a) A contractor for whom postponing concreting costs ₹50,000, while rain on fresh unprotected concrete would cause damage of ₹60,000.
(b) An event organiser for whom hiring a covered tent costs ₹1,00,000, while rain on an open-air event would cause losses of ₹1,50,000.
(c) A farmer for whom delaying a spray costs ₹5,000, while a spray washed off by rain would waste ₹8,000.
(d) A salt-pan worker for whom covering the pans costs ₹2,000, while unprotected rain would destroy salt worth ₹20,000.
explanation: The passage sets each user's threshold at cost of protection ÷ loss if unprotected; protection is worthwhile when the probability exceeds it. Ratios: (a) 0.83, (b) 0.67, (c) 0.625, (d) 0.10. Only in (d) is 0.30 above the threshold. (A data-science reader will recognise the classic cost–loss decision model: act if p > C/L.)
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Inference - applying the cost/loss threshold to new cases

Q. The author's criticism that a categorical forecast "silently imposes a single threshold on everyone" assumes which one of the following?
options: (a) Users of forecasts differ materially in the cost of protecting themselves relative to the loss they would suffer unprotected.
(b) Forecasters are less competent than users at interpreting model output.
(c) Probabilistic forecasts are right more often than categorical forecasts.
(d) Users will always act on the official forecast rather than on their own experience.

subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Assumption - negation test on the 'single threshold' criticism

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

We praise originality as though it were the opposite of imitation, and tend to regard the imitator as someone who has not yet found himself. Yet it is hard to name any capacity we did not acquire by copying. The child learns to speak by reproducing sounds whose meaning it does not yet grasp; the apprentice learns a craft by repeating movements whose purpose becomes clear only later; the young writer learns to write by composing, often unconsciously, in the manner of writers she admires. At each stage the learner submits to a form she did not choose and could not yet have chosen, because the standards by which one might choose are themselves part of what is being learnt.

It does not follow that originality is an illusion. It follows that originality is a late achievement, and a relational one. A new idea is new only against a background of the old; a departure from convention is intelligible only to those who know the convention, including the one who departs. The composer who breaks a rule of harmony must first hear why the rule was there, or his breach is not a discovery but an accident. Those who are impatient to be original and refuse the discipline of imitation do not escape influence; they merely submit to the influences that are most widespread and least examined, and end up sounding like everyone else.

What distinguishes the mature practitioner is not that she has ceased to imitate but that she imitates knowingly and selectively. She has taken in enough of a tradition to see its tensions — the places where its own standards pull against one another — and her innovations typically come from pressing on those points. The self we call original is, in this sense, less a possession than a way of standing within an inheritance: close enough to be formed by it, far enough to argue with it.

Q. Which one of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: (a) Originality is an illusion, since every human capacity is acquired by copying.
(b) Learners should reproduce their teachers' methods exactly until they have mastered every rule of a craft.
(c) Originality is not the opposite of imitation but grows out of a disciplined, and eventually critical, engagement with a tradition.
(d) Every tradition contains internal tensions, which make innovation inevitable.
explanation: The author explicitly denies (a) ('It does not follow that originality is an illusion'); (b) overstates — the mature practitioner imitates 'selectively'; (d) is a supporting detail and 'inevitable' is too strong. (c) states the thesis: originality is a late, relational achievement.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Main idea - originality as a relational achievement within a tradition

Q. On the author's view, which one of the following persons is most likely to produce work that is least original?
options: (a) A painter who trained for years in classical technique and now deliberately distorts perspective to question classical ideals.
(b) A poet who refuses to read other poets for fear of being influenced, and whose verse ends up closely resembling the popular songs of the day.
(c) A scientist who notices that two accepted theories in her field make conflicting predictions and designs an experiment to settle the matter.
(d) A musician who learned by transcribing the solos of masters and now combines their styles in unfamiliar ways.
explanation: The passage says those who refuse the discipline of imitation 'submit to the influences that are most widespread and least examined, and end up sounding like everyone else' — exactly (b). (a) and (d) are knowing, selective imitation; (c) is 'pressing on' a tradition's internal tensions.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Inference - author's likely judgement on cases

(d) contemptuous of every attempt at innovation.

subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Tone and attitude - towards the impatiently original

question:
Six persons — P, Q, R, S, T and U — sit in a single row, all facing north.
(i) Q sits at one of the extreme ends.
(ii) Exactly two persons sit between Q and P.
(iii) U sits immediately to the right of P.
(iv) S sits immediately to the left of Q.
(v) R does not sit at either end.

Q. Which pair sits at the two extreme ends of the row?
explanation: Number seats 1–6 from left to right (facing north, 'right' = higher number). From (i)–(ii): Q = 1 with P = 4, or Q = 6 with P = 3. From (iv) S must be immediately left of Q, which is impossible if Q = 1; so Q = 6, S = 5, P = 3, and by (iii) U = 4. T and R fill seats 1 and 2; by (v) R = 2, T = 1. Row: T R P U S Q. Ends: T and Q.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Linear seating arrangement (single row, facing north)

question: 15 August 2026 falls on a Saturday. On which day of the week will 15 August 2030 fall?
explanation: Count odd days year by year from 15 Aug to 15 Aug: 2026→27: 365 days = 1; 2027→28: includes 29 Feb 2028 = 2; 2028→29: 1; 2029→30: 1. Total 5 odd days. Saturday + 5 = Thursday. Trap: forgetting the leap day gives 4 → Wednesday; counting 2026's own February (already past) is the other common slip.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Calendar - odd days across a leap year

question:
Statements: P ≥ Q > R;  S < R ≤ T;  U = Q
Conclusions:
I. P > S
II. T > Q
III. U > S

Which of the conclusions definitely follow?
explanation: I: P ≥ Q > R > S → P > S ✔. II: T ≥ R and Q > R, but T and Q are not linked — cannot be determined ✘. III: U = Q > R > S → U > S ✔. Hence only I and III.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Coded inequalities - chained comparisons

question:
A die has its faces numbered 1 to 6. It is shown in two positions:
Position 1 — Top: 1, Front: 2, Right: 3
Position 2 — Top: 1, Front: 4, Right: 2

Which number is on the face opposite to 3?
explanation: Face 1 is on top in both positions, so the four side faces form a fixed cycle (front → right → back → left) when viewed from above. Position 1 gives the cycle (2, 3, x, y). Position 2 is the same die rotated about the vertical axis: front 4 is followed by right 2, so 4 comes immediately before 2 in the cycle — i.e. y = 4 and x = 5. Cycle: 2, 3, 5, 4. Opposite pairs: 2–5, 3–4, and 1–6. So 4 is opposite 3. Trap: (c) 5 is opposite 2, not 3.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Dice - deducing opposite faces from two positions with orientation

question:
If '+' means '×', '−' means '÷', '×' means '−' and '÷' means '+', and the numbers 3 and 6 are also interchanged, what is the value of:

18 − 3 + 4 ÷ 6 × 5
explanation: Swap 3 and 6: 18 − 6 + 4 ÷ 3 × 5. Replace symbols: 18 ÷ 6 × 4 + 3 − 5. BODMAS: 18 ÷ 6 = 3; 3 × 4 = 12; 12 + 3 − 5 = 10. Trap (a) 25 comes from ignoring the number swap (18 ÷ 3 × 4 + 6 − 5).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Mathematical operations - symbol and number interchange

question:
Statement: Should it be made mandatory for all private hospitals to display the rates of common treatments and procedures publicly?
Arguments:
I. Yes. It will allow patients to compare costs and make informed choices before treatment.
II. No. Private hospitals are privately owned and the government should not interfere in their affairs.
III. Yes. Hospitals in many developed countries already do so.

Which of the arguments is/are strong?
explanation: I is strong: it is directly relevant and names a real benefit (informed choice, lower information asymmetry). II is weak: it is a sweeping claim — health care is a legitimately regulated sector. III is weak: 'others do it' is imitation, not a reason tied to the merits.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Strong and weak arguments

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

Price index and quantity sold of a commodity (price index base: 2020 = 100; price in 2020 = ₹40 per kg)

| Year | Price index | Quantity sold ('000 tonnes) |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 100 | 50 |
| 2021 | 112 | 52 |
| 2022 | 126 | 48 |
| 2023 | 120 | 55 |
| 2024 | 134 | 54 |
| 2025 | 150 | 60 |

Q. In which year was the percentage increase in the price over the previous year the highest?
explanation: Growth = index ÷ previous index − 1: 2021: 12/100 = 12.0%; 2022: 14/112 = 12.5%; 2023: fall; 2024: 14/120 = 11.7%; 2025: 16/134 = 11.9%. Highest is 2022. Trap (d): 2025 has the largest rise in index points (16) but on a larger base. Shortcut: compare 14/112 = 1/8 with 16/134 < 1/8.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Index numbers - year-on-year percentage change vs absolute change (trap)

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

Price index and quantity sold of a commodity (price index base: 2020 = 100; price in 2020 = ₹40 per kg)

| Year | Price index | Quantity sold ('000 tonnes) |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 100 | 50 |
| 2021 | 112 | 52 |
| 2022 | 126 | 48 |
| 2023 | 120 | 55 |
| 2024 | 134 | 54 |
| 2025 | 150 | 60 |

Q. By what percentage was the sales revenue from the commodity in 2025 higher than in 2020?
explanation: Revenue ∝ price index × quantity. 2020: 100 × 50 = 5,000; 2025: 150 × 60 = 9,000. Ratio 1.8 → 80% higher. (In rupees: ₹40/kg × 5 crore kg = ₹200 crore vs ₹60/kg × 6 crore kg = ₹360 crore.) Trap (a): adding 50% price growth and 20% quantity growth ignores the cross term 0.5 × 0.2 = 10%.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Index numbers - revenue change from price and quantity together

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

Season record of five batsmen (batting average = runs ÷ number of times dismissed, where times dismissed = innings − not outs)

| Batsman | Innings | Not outs | Runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 20 | 4 | 640 |
| B | 18 | 0 | 684 |
| C | 22 | 6 | 672 |
| D | 15 | 3 | 540 |
| E | 24 | 2 | 814 |

Q. Which batsman has the highest batting average?
explanation: Averages (runs ÷ dismissals): A 640/16 = 40; B 684/18 = 38; C 672/16 = 42; D 540/12 = 45; E 814/22 = 37. D is highest. Trap (a): B has the highest runs per innings (38) because he has no not-outs — dividing by innings instead of dismissals gives B.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Averages with a changed denominator (runs per dismissal vs per innings)

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

Season record of five batsmen (batting average = runs ÷ number of times dismissed, where times dismissed = innings − not outs)

| Batsman | Innings | Not outs | Runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 20 | 4 | 640 |
| B | 18 | 0 | 684 |
| C | 22 | 6 | 672 |
| D | 15 | 3 | 540 |
| E | 24 | 2 | 814 |

Q. How many runs must E score in his next innings, in which he is dismissed, to raise his batting average to exactly 38?
explanation: E's current average = 814/22 = 37. After one more dismissal he has 23 dismissals, so he needs 38 × 23 = 874 runs in all: 874 − 814 = 60. Shortcut: he needs 38 for the new innings plus 1 extra for each of the 22 earlier dismissals = 60. Trap (c) 136 uses innings (25) instead of dismissals.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Required value to reach a target average

question: You are the Block Development Officer. A sanctioned all-weather road will connect several tribal hamlets to the block headquarters. When surveyors arrive, villagers refuse them entry; a rumour is circulating that the road is a pretext to take their land for a mining company. The work is already behind schedule. What is the best course of action?
options: (a) Ask for police protection so that the survey can be completed on schedule, since the project is legally sanctioned.

(b) Meet the gram sabha and village elders with an interpreter, explain the alignment, the land actually required, compensation and their legal rights, answer the rumour with facts, and involve local representatives in the survey itself.
(c) Postpone the project indefinitely until the villagers approach the administration themselves.
(d) Offer a few influential villagers personal incentives to persuade the others.
explanation: (b) addresses the real problem — mistrust and misinformation — through transparency, respect for the gram sabha's role and participation, while still moving the project forward. (a) uses coercion and deepens mistrust; (c) abandons a public good; (d) is unethical inducement.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Community consent and trust-building in a tribal area

question: Two days before a beneficiary list for a housing scheme is to be sent to the district, you discover that a newly joined assistant has made a data-entry error that omits about 40 eligible families. The assistant is conscientious but anxious. What should you do?
options: (a) Correct the list yourself quietly and send it, without mentioning the error to anyone.
(b) Report the assistant to the district office for disciplinary action.
(c) Send the list as it is to meet the deadline and submit a correction later.

(d) Work with the assistant to correct and re-verify the list before the deadline, explain the check that was missed, introduce a cross-verification step for future lists, and inform your superior if the deadline needs a short extension.
explanation: (d) protects the 40 families, meets or transparently manages the deadline, builds the assistant's capacity and fixes the process. (a) loses the learning and hides a systemic gap; (b) is disproportionate for an honest first error; (c) knowingly transmits a list that excludes eligible people.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Accountability and mentoring after a subordinate's error

question: In a review meeting chaired by your superior, a fellow officer presents an analysis that you prepared and shared with him, without acknowledging you. The superior praises him. What is the most appropriate response?
options: (a) After the meeting, speak to the colleague privately to clear up the matter; if needed, ensure in a matter-of-fact way that your superior has an accurate record of how the work was prepared, keeping the focus on the work rather than on grievance.
(b) Interrupt the meeting and point out publicly that the work is yours.
(c) Say nothing now or later, since credit does not matter in public service.
(d) Stop sharing your work with colleagues in future.
explanation: (a) is proportionate: it gives the colleague a chance to correct it, keeps the record honest and preserves working relationships. (b) embarrasses everyone publicly; (c) allows misrepresentation to stand; (d) harms teamwork and the organisation.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Credit-taking by a peer - professional conduct

question: How many divisors of 720 are perfect squares (including 1)?
explanation: 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5. A square divisor needs even exponents: 2 ∈ {0, 2, 4} (3 ways), 3 ∈ {0, 2} (2 ways), 5 ∈ {0} (1 way). Total 3 × 2 × 1 = 6: 1, 4, 9, 16, 36, 144.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Number theory - perfect-square divisors

question: A shopkeeper marks his goods 40% above cost price and allows successive discounts of 10% and 5%. He also uses a false weight, giving 900 g when he claims to give 1 kg. What is his overall profit percentage?
explanation: Let cost be ₹100 per kg. Price charged for a 'kg' = 100 × 1.40 × 0.90 × 0.95 = ₹119.70. Goods actually given = 0.9 kg, costing ₹90. Profit % = 119.70/90 − 1 = 1.33 − 1 = 33%. Trap (b) 19.7% ignores the false weight; (c) 29.7% adds the 10% from the weight instead of compounding it.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Profit and loss - mark-up, successive discounts and false weight

question: A and B start together from the same point on a circular track of length 600 m and run in opposite directions at constant speeds of 5 m/s and 7 m/s respectively. At how many distinct points on the track will they meet if they keep running indefinitely?
explanation: Opposite directions: relative speed 12 m/s, so they meet every 600/12 = 50 s, A advancing 250 m each time. A's meeting positions are 250k mod 600: 0, 250, 500, 150, 400, 50, 300, 550, 200, 450, 100, 350, then back to 0 — 12 distinct points. Rule: with speeds in lowest ratio a:b (here 5:7), opposite directions give a + b distinct points; same direction gives |a − b| (= 2, trap (a)).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Circular track - distinct meeting points (opposite directions)
